query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Tailoring the heat treatment profile to enhance Al diffusion in high-entropy alloys will promote the rapid formation and sustained adherence of a continuous, protective alumina (Al2O3) scale during high-temperature exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (e.g., FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 or similar) with a homogeneous, supersaturated BCC solid solution containing sufficient Al for oxide formation.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat or thermomechanical treatment designed to optimize temperature-time profiles that accelerate Al diffusion toward the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation environment (e.g., exposure in air at temperatures between 700 °C and 900 °C) under controlled oxygen partial pressures.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced Al diffusion kinetics, which leads to localized Al enrichment at the surface and subsequent nucleation and growth of a continuous alumina layer.
generation.mechanism: The tailored heat treatment promotes faster Al transport from the subsurface to the surface. This increased flux of Al speeds up the formation of a coherent, adherent alumina (Al2O3) layer that acts as a diffusion barrier, mitigating further oxidation and phase transformations in the underlying alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional heat treatment, the tailored treatment will yield an alloy that exhibits a more uniform, continuous, and adherent alumina scale with lower overall oxide thickness and reduced oxidation mass gain. These improvements indicate enhanced oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: Identical high-entropy alloy samples subjected to a conventional heat treatment profile without optimized Al diffusion control.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to high-entropy alloys with appreciable Al content and within high-temperature oxidation regimes (700–900 °C) in oxidizing atmospheres. Its effectiveness may be limited if the alloy composition or processing conditions do not favor a BCC matrix or if other competing diffusion mechanisms dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance (e.g., percentage reduction in mass gain or oxide scale thickness) and the robustness of this effect across varying oxygen partial pressures and alloy compositions remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples with identical compositions. Subject one set to a conventional heat treatment and the other to the tailored heat treatment designed to maximize Al diffusion. Expose both sets to a high-temperature oxidation environment (e.g., air at 800 °C for a fixed time).
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (SEM imaging/EDS mapping)
Phase identification and integrity of the protective scale (XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tailored treatment does not produce a statistically significant improvement (i.e., more uniform and thinner alumina scale, lower mass gain, and improved phase stability) compared to the conventional treatment under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that optimizing Al diffusion via tailored heat treatment enhances oxidation resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Oxidation and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder produced via gas atomization were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. The following was found:Under HVOF spraying, the processes of oxidation and phase transformations occur in the following sequence: (i) pronounced Al diffusion from subsurface BCC supersaturated solid solution to the particle surface; (ii) particle’s surface Al2O3 formation; and (iii) FCC formation in the Al-depleted subsurface layer.During continuous heating in an air atmosphere, processes occur in the following sequence: (i) decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation; (ii) Al diffusion to the surface; and (iii) simultaneous formation of Al2O3 and FCC due to Al outflow from BCC/B2.During prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C in an air atmosphere, processes occur in the following sequence: (i) decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation; (ii) diffusion of Al, Cr, Fe, and Mo to the surface; and (iii) formation of surface Al2O3 and undersurface sigma due to enrichment of the undersurface zone with Cr

reading.lever: Tailor heat treatment profiles to control Al diffusion, ensuring rapid formation and sustained adherence of a continuous alumina layer.
reading.why: Because optimizing the kinetics of Al transport at high temperatures directly promotes the formation and retention of a protective oxide scale, mitigating non-uniformity and phase instability issues observed in prior studies.
